findings.explanation: ATS is relaxed for a class of connections (web content, media, or local-network addresses), permitting cleartext or weak-TLS loads of that traffic. MASTG-TEST-0322 fails on each of these keys.
findings.remediation: Drop NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsInWebContent, NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsForMedia and NSAllowsLocalNetworking where not needed and load the content over HTTPS. If a specific host needs cleartext, scope it under NSExceptionDomains instead.
findings.title: ATS relaxed for web, media or local-network content (NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsInWebContent, NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsForMedia)
findings.why: Same weakness as the global opt-out, scoped to web content, media or local resources (unqualified and .local names, IP addresses), so less of the app's data is exposed. IP addresses can be anywhere on the internet, so the attack vector stays network.

findings.title: Calendar / Reminders access (EventKit)
findings.why: A calendar is a diary, which WP248 criterion 4 lists by name ("personal documents, emails, diaries"). One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.title: Contacts (ABAddressBook / CNContactStore)

findings.title: Photo library (PHPhotoLibrary)
findings.why: The photo library holds personal documents and the location each photo was taken, data of a highly personal nature under WP248 criterion 4. One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.explanation: UIPasteboard / generalPasteboard / UIPasteboardChanged, reading the system pasteboard. Background clipboard reads are a well-documented privacy issue.
findings.title: UIPasteboard / generalPasteboard access
findings.why: Access to a store of personal data. The contact list, pasteboard and media library are not among the WP248 high-risk criteria; photos and calendars are scored on their own rules.

findings.explanation: Direct reads from CMMotionManager / CMAccelerometer / CMGyro, used for gait analysis and behavioural fingerprinting.
findings.title: CoreMotion accelerometer / gyroscope
findings.why: Motion and touch input. Raw sensor access meets none of the WP248 criteria unless an SDK scores the person with it.

findings.explanation: LocalAuthentication / LAPolicy biometric checks. The app receives only success or failure, never biometric data. Whether the check is event-bound (MASWE-0020) needs the evaluatePolicy call site, which sits in encrypted code, so this records the API for review and is not a weakness on its own.
findings.title: FaceID / LocalAuthentication biometrics
findings.why: LocalAuthentication returns only success or failure; no biometric data reaches the app (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/localauthentication). Whether the check is event-bound and bypassable (MASWE-0020) depends on the evaluatePolicy call site MASTG-TEST-0266 reads, which FairPlay encrypts, so the rule records the API and nothing more.

findings.why: Camera and screen capture APIs. Capture alone meets none of the WP248 criteria.

findings.explanation: Calls -[UIApplication canOpenURL:] or declares LSApplicationQueriesSchemes, used to test which other apps are installed (iOS analogue of Android's QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES).
findings.title: canOpenURL / LSApplicationQueriesSchemes runtime probe
findings.why: One canOpenURL call is not enumeration.

findings.explanation: The app declares URL schemes it can probe with -canOpenURL:, the iOS analogue of Android's QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES. A short list (deep-linking into a few partner apps) is routine; a long list is an installed-app fingerprinting signal.
findings.remediation: Trim LSApplicationQueriesSchemes to only the apps you genuinely interoperate with; probing a broad list to fingerprint installed apps risks App Store rejection.
findings.title: Probes installed apps via LSApplicationQueriesSchemes (6 schemes)
findings.why: Which apps are installed says what a person is interested in: WP248 criterion 1 covers profiling from "personal preferences or interests". One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.why: The connected network's BSSID locates the device. Location data: WP248 criterion 4 names it among data of a highly personal nature ("location data whose collection questions the freedom of movement"). One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.title: Runtime JavaScript evaluation in WebView
findings.why: The app evaluates JavaScript in its WebView.

findings.explanation: Adding a WKScriptMessageHandler creates a JS→native call channel. Combined with a remote page, this lets a server invoke native methods.
findings.title: WKScriptMessageHandler JS→native bridge
findings.why: A JS-to-native bridge exists. What matters is what it exposes, which needs the two rules above to say.

findings.explanation: WKUserScript injects JS at document start/end on every load, useful for telemetry and credential interception.
findings.title: WKUserScript injection
findings.why: The app injects a user script into its WebView.

findings.explanation: Calls the isInspectable setter of WKWebView or JSContext (iOS 16.4+). When the value is true in a release build, Safari Web Inspector can attach over USB. The scan sees the call; the value is in FairPlay-encrypted code.
findings.title: Web Inspector toggle set on a WebView or JavaScript context (isInspectable)
findings.why: The isInspectable setter of a WebView or JavaScript context is called. Safari Web Inspector attaches only when the value is true in the release build; the value is in FairPlay-encrypted code, so the scan records the call (MASWE-0063).

findings.explanation: WKWebView is the iOS embedded browser.
findings.title: WKWebView in use
findings.why: The app embeds a WebView.

findings.explanation: The app registers custom URL scheme(s) via CFBundleURLSchemes. Any app or web page can invoke these; if application(_:open:options:) acts on unvalidated parameters, this is an entry point for unauthorized actions. Custom schemes are also unverified (unlike Universal Links). Review the handler for input validation.
findings.remediation: Validate and sanitize every parameter in application(_:open:options:); never trigger sensitive actions from a URL without authentication. Prefer Universal Links (verified) over custom schemes.
findings.title: Registers 4 custom URL schemes (inbound deep-link surface)
findings.why: The app registers custom URL schemes. MASWE-0029 makes them a weakness when a sensitive flow relies on them or the handler does not validate input, which MASTG-TEST-0370 and -0371 read from the handler code.

findings.explanation: Legal iOS background-execution channels. `location`/`voip` enable persistent background execution and are the strongest signal; `audio`/`external-accessory` are moderate; `fetch`/`remote-notification`/`processing` are routine and declared by most apps.
findings.remediation: Declare only the background modes the app actually needs; each is reviewed by App Review and must map to genuine user-facing functionality, not background telemetry.
findings.title: Background modes declared: audio, remote-notification, voip
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.explanation: VoIP background mode keeps the app alive indefinitely.
findings.title: UIBackgroundModes contains "voip"
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.title: Communication-style push
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.explanation: content-available=1 silent push lets the server wake the app to refresh data without a visible notification. The `didReceiveRemoteNotification` delegate method appears in almost every push-using app, so it's no longer a primary signal; the silent variant is the `content-available` payload and the `remote-notification` UIBackgroundModes entry together.
findings.title: Content-available silent push
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.explanation: PushKit lets a server wake the app at any time without notifying the user, used by legitimate VoIP, but also as a covert wakeup channel. Apple has tightened policy several times; restricted to actual VoIP calls.
findings.title: PushKit VoIP push (silent wakeup)
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.explanation: The bundle contains http:// URLs for 1 host(s): tizen.org. A hard-coded cleartext URL is a place the app may talk to a server without TLS. Whether it does depends on how the URL is used and on the ATS configuration, which blocks cleartext loads through URLSession unless an exception allows them.
findings.remediation: Switch each URL to https://, and remove any ATS exception that only exists to keep a cleartext endpoint working.
findings.title: Hard-coded cleartext http:// URLs (1 host)
findings.why: MASTG notes that an http:// URL in the bundle does not show it is used for communication; the scan records the candidates.

findings.explanation: References NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey / isExcludedFromBackup. The key does not guarantee exclusion, and sensitive files still need to be encrypted, so its presence is a reference, not a mitigation.
findings.title: Backup-exclusion API in use (NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey)
findings.why: Records that the app marks files as excluded from backup.

findings.explanation: A binary imports NSFileProtectionNone, the class that leaves a file readable while the device is locked. The import shows the option is referenced, often by a library that maps every protection class; whether it is applied to sensitive data needs the manual review the linked MASTG test describes.
findings.title: References NSFileProtectionNone
findings.why: The import shows the protection class is referenced, not that sensitive data is stored under it.

findings.explanation: Imports rand() / srand() / random() / drand48(), predictable PRNGs unsuitable for tokens, keys, IVs or nonces. Use SecRandomCopyBytes or arc4random_buf. `arc4random() % n` also introduces modulo bias; prefer arc4random_uniform(n).
findings.title: Non-cryptographic random number generator
findings.why: A non-cryptographic generator is linked. MASTG-TEST-0311 fails only when its output is used for keys, tokens or other security values, which is in FairPlay-encrypted code, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: Imports CC_MD5 / CC_SHA1 (CommonCrypto) or CryptoKit's Insecure.MD5 / Insecure.SHA1. Both are collision-broken and unsuitable for signatures, integrity checks or password hashing, but are also widely used for non-security purposes (cache keys, ETags, file checksums), so the finding is a pointer for review.
findings.title: Weak hash primitive (MD5 / SHA-1)
findings.why: MD5 or SHA-1 is linked. MASTG-TEST-0211 fails only when the hash protects sensitive data; checksums and cache keys pass. That use is in FairPlay-encrypted code, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: Binaries carrying 5186 debugger (stab) entries in their symbol table: DTBiOSSDK, MobileFuseSDK, NGSDK, SurveyMonkeyiOSSDK. Stabs name source files, object files and functions, and often the build machine's paths. They make reverse engineering easier and are not needed to run the app.
findings.remediation: Set Debug Information Format to DWARF with dSYM File for release builds and keep the dSYM out of the app bundle; strip the binaries.
findings.title: Debug symbols left in binaries (4)
findings.why: Leftover debug information eases reverse engineering; MASWE files it under the resilience profile, where it is a finding only when resilience is required.

findings.explanation: No __stack_chk_* symbols were found in a binary that carries Objective-C metadata. Stack canaries mitigate stack buffer overflows, but a Swift class that subclasses an Objective-C class also carries that metadata and Swift code rarely needs a canary, so MASTG-TEST-0229 treats this as a lead for manual review of the build flags, not as a result.
findings.remediation: Rebuild with -fstack-protector-strong (or -fstack-protector-all) so the compiler inserts stack canaries on functions with local buffers.
findings.title: No stack-canary symbol found: WidgetExtension
findings.why: No __stack_chk_* symbol in a binary that carries Objective-C metadata. MASTG-TEST-0229 lists expected false positives for this check (Swift code, Flutter, React Native, compiler optimisation) and asks for the source and build flags to decide, so the binary is recorded for review.

findings.explanation: application-groups entitlement allows multiple apps from the same publisher to share UserDefaults/files (often used to share IDFA / VPN-detected flag between sibling apps).
findings.title: App Groups entitlement (cross-app data sharing)
findings.why: Shared container between the vendor's own apps.

findings.explanation: aps-environment entitlement, push notifications.
findings.title: APS push environment
findings.why: Push environment the build targets.

findings.explanation: The binary imports dlopen/dlsym, so it can resolve and call code chosen at runtime rather than at link time. That is how optional frameworks, plugin architectures and A/B-tested SDKs are loaded, and it is entirely normal, so this ships as INFO inventory rather than a weakness. It matters only as context: an app that also carries obfuscation (SURV-04) or a data broker (TRK-02) can assemble behaviour a static scan cannot see, and dynamic code loading is the mechanism that makes that possible. Note the limit of the signal: an import proves the symbol is linked, not that it is ever called, and iOS forbids loading code that is not already in the signed bundle. (MASWE-0049)
findings.title: Dynamic loader in use (dlopen / dlsym)
findings.why: dlopen/dlsym are present in the binary.

findings.explanation: com.apple.developer.associated-domains, handles universal links / web credentials.
findings.title: Associated domains / universal links
findings.why: Associated domains the app claims.

findings.explanation: The app declares com.apple.developer.devicecheck.appattest-environment, so it uses App Attest to prove to its own server that requests come from a genuine, unmodified build. findings.title: App Attest / DeviceCheck attestation in use (positive signal)
findings.why: A positive signal: the app attests itself to its backend.

findings.explanation: Uses the Keychain Services API (SecItemAdd / SecItemCopyMatching / SecItemUpdate). Informational, pair with SECH-02.keychain_accessible_always to judge whether items are protected with an appropriate accessibility / access-control class.
findings.title: Keychain API in use (SecItem)
findings.why: A positive signal: the app uses the Keychain.

findings.explanation: Third-party code from Amazon (US) is embedded via 1 SDK(s): Amazon Ads (APS). Each embedded SDK is a supply-chain dependency that can collect data and update its own behaviour.

findings.explanation: Imports the C function getifaddrs() which lists every network interface. NOTE: getifaddrs is also the standard primitive for plain reachability and local-IP discovery and is linked by many networking SDKs, so the import alone is a weak VPN signal that fires on most apps. findings.explanation: Hard-codes paths that exist only on jailbroken devices. The narrow primary pattern targets paths that are *only* jailbreak-relevant (Cydia, apt, the MobileSubstrate dylibs and jailbreakd). Broader literals such as `/bin/bash` or `/etc/apt` regularly appear in stock debug strings and are handled by the `ignore-stdlib-debug-paths` suppression; they only re-surface when these higher-signal paths also appear in the same binary.

findings.explanation: Across the bundle's privacy manifests the app and its SDKs declare collecting: AdvertisingData, CoarseLocation, CrashData, DeviceID, EmailAddress, Name, OtherDataTypes, OtherDiagnosticData, OtherUsageData, PerformanceData, PhoneNumber, PreciseLocation, ProductInteraction, UserID. 11 are declared linked to the user's identity and 6 used for tracking. findings.explanation: The app ships a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy declaring 3 tracking domain(s), but 16 further tracker-classified hosts appear in the bundle and are not covered by any declaration (Amazon, Google, PubMatic, Taboola, Verve). iOS makes requests to the domains listed in NSPrivacyTrackingDomains fail when the user has not granted App Tracking Transparency permission; a tracking domain missing from the list is not blocked, so the user's choice does not reach it. A domain is treated as declared when it matches exactly or is a subdomain of a declared entry. MASTG-TEST-0281 fails on exactly this.
findings.remediation: Add every host that carries tracking traffic to NSPrivacyTrackingDomains, or stop contacting it on a tracking code path. Apple's guidance is that the list must cover the domains the app reaches for tracking purposes, not just the SDKs it recognises.
findings.title: 16 tracker domains reached but not declared in the privacy manifest
findings.why: The manifest declares tracking domains but misses some the app reaches, which fails MASTG-TEST-0281. iOS blocks only the declared domains when ATT permission is withheld, so the missing ones keep working. A declaration gap against Apple's rules and GDPR Art. 13; no standard grades it, so it is info.

findings.explanation: The bundle references 8 endpoint(s) whose owner is based in DE, owners: Verve. The country is the owning organisation's home jurisdiction from the tracker database, not where a server is hosted, and a referenced endpoint is not observed traffic. If the app sends personal data there, it is a third-country transfer: whether that is lawful depends on the safeguards, purpose and paperwork behind it, none of which is visible in a binary. DE holds an EU adequacy decision, so a transfer there needs no additional Chapter V safeguard. Tracker-class endpoints are among the destinations.

findings.explanation: The main Mach-O is encrypted by the App Store. Static string scanning of its TEXT segment won't work without a decrypted dump (e.g., via frida-ios-dump or bagbak on a jailbroken device). Embedded frameworks and dylibs are USUALLY ENCRYPTED TOO (measured 91% across the reference corpus; in half of apps every Mach-O is encrypted), so TEXT-segment string recall is limited bundle-wide, not just for the main binary. What still survives encryption is __LINKEDIT: symbols, imported/defined symbol names, ObjC selectors and linked dylibs, which is why symbol-based detection carries this scan rather than string matching.
findings.remediation: For full TEXT-segment coverage, supply a decrypted .ipa produced by frida-ios-dump or bagbak from a jailbroken device. Resource files, plists, entitlements, symbols, selectors and linked dylibs are still scanned in the meantime.
findings.title: Main executable is FairPlay-encrypted
findings.why: Scan metadata: what the scanner could and could not see.
